logline: In a near-future Britain where androids called Synths do domestic labour, a family discovers their new Synth carries secret memories - and the question of what counts as consciousness begins to cost people everything.

renewal.note: Channel 4 announced in May 2019 that a fourth series would not be commissioned. The show concluded after three series with the societal implications of Synth consciousness left deliberately unresolved.

bollymeter.basis: An 89% RT score from 62 critics who found it a thoughtful, well-acted Asimov riff - the show earns its premise through character rather than spectacle, though it rarely breaks beyond the philosophical territory it inherits from decades of AI fiction.

seasons.review_body: Humans premiered on Channel 4 in June 2015, adapted from the Swedish series Real Humans by Jonathan Brackley and Sam Vincent. The opening week brought 5.4 million viewers, making it the highest rated new drama on Channel 4 that year. The 89 percent Rotten Tomatoes score from 62 reviews points to strong overall appreciation, alongside the sense that the show operates within familiar AI conscious territory. What distinguished it was the casting: Gemma Chan's Mia is the emotional centre of the Synth storyline, her restrained performance conveying inner life without melodrama. Katherine Parkinson grounds the domestic subplot in something recognisably human. The series is noted for asking real questions about personhood, consent, and labour without fully settling any of them, a pattern that held through 2015 and later felt like mild frustration by Season 3.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere builds the Synth world in the background while keeping the foreground domestic and recognisable: a family buying an android helper and discovering that the product they purchased is more than the catalogue described. The show's restraint in its pilot is its biggest early achievement - it does not rush to declare what it is, letting the uncanny accumulate.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Anita's eyes in the kitchen at night - the moment the show commits to the idea that this is not a horror story but something harder to classify.

bollymeter.basis: 94% on RT from 17 critics with the consensus that it quietly distinguishes itself from flashier AI competition - the show broadened its societal focus and the Synth ensemble became stronger as individual characters developed.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 aired on Channel 4 in October 2016. The Synth civil rights framing, with conscious Synths navigating a world designed to deny their personhood, moved to the foreground. Gemma Chan and Colin Morgan anchored the Synth storylines while the Hawkins family stayed the human access point. The season builds on the world rules established in Season 1 and then tests and pushes against them. The show is doing quieter work than most AI dramas of the period, with restraint that keeps the focus on character and consequence.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 expands the societal dimension of the Synth consciousness question and gives the non-human characters more structural weight than the domestic household storyline.

bollymeter.basis: 100% on RT from 13 critics, though the audience score dropped to 78% - the sociopolitical ambition of the final season outpaced its narrative resolution, and cancellation before the story completed left the show without the closing argument it had earned.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 aired from May 2018 on Channel 4, earning a perfect 100 percent Rotten Tomatoes score based on 13 critics. The season’s expanded sociopolitical scope, with Synths integrated into and then violently expelled from public life, delivers its most ambitious storytelling yet. The show uses immigration policy, identity documentation, and labor rights as real-world analogues without turning into a simple parable. Rotten Tomatoes audience scores held at 78 percent, reflecting mixed feelings about the closing arc: the season ends without resolution because the cancellation announcement came mid story. The new societal dimensions deepen the character work, even as the end leaves viewers frustrated by the lack of a payoff after three seasons of careful world building.
seasons.season_over_season: The most sociopolitically engaged season and arguably the most ambitious. The cancellation truncated an arc that needed completion.
